articles.title: Ukraine launches over 1,000 drones at Russia, setting oil facilities ablaze
articles.summary: The air strike, one of Ukraine’s largest in the war, comes amid rising tensions between Kyiv and Washington.
articles.body:
At least one person has been killed, and five others injured after Ukraine launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia, one of Kyiv’s largest aerial strikes in the war.

St Petersburg Governor Alexander Beglov said firefighters were battling fires sparked by Sunday’s attacks on the St Petersburg oil terminal, the Ruchi oil depot and industrial warehouses in the Kolpinsky district south of the city.

The governor said the “massive” strike killed at least one person and injured five, and that several residential buildings and two houses were also hit.

The attack disrupted flights at St Petersburg’s main airport, one of the country’s busiest, which was restricting operations “for safety reasons”, Beglov said.

Russian e-commerce company Ozon said there was a fire at its logistics hub in St Petersburg. The internet company VK said drones attacked its data centre in the broader Leningrad region, adding that normal services were available to users.

Leningrad Governor Alexander Drozdenko said 145 drones had been shot down and about 20,000 people were without electricity following the drone raid.

The Ministry of Defence said 1,015 Ukrainian drones were neutralised overnight over 15 Russian regions, the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black Sea.

The strikes came as tensions between Kyiv and Washington deepened, with US President Donald Trump criticising Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil infrastructure, and the prospect of further US sanctions against Moscow still uncertain.

On Sunday, Trump defended his Friday decision to put a hold on implementing new sanctions on Russia, saying he did not want to do anything that would “foolishly” drive Moscow “away from the bargaining table”.

In a social media post, the US president said he believed new sanctions would undermine negotiations to bring about a diplomatic end to Moscow’s war on Ukraine, refuting bipartisan criticism that he was favouring Russian President Vladimir Putin’s interests over Kyiv’s.

Trump also lashed out at Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who has been critical of Trump’s recent outreach to Putin, for launching strikes on Russian energy infrastructure, claiming Zelenskyy “doesn’t want to end this war”.

Trump had announced on October 11 that Russia and Ukraine agreed to an “energy ceasefire” , but offered no details. Zelenskyy told The Financial Times that he was “done” with the ceasefire a few days later, after holding off on striking Russia’s energy facilities while Moscow had continued attacking Ukraine’s.

Zelenskyy wrote on X on Sunday that Russia had attacked Ukraine’s energy, oil and gas sectors 76 times in the week since Trump’s announcement.

Energy facilities in four Ukrainian regions were struck overnight, leaving tens of thousands of families without power, he said, accusing Russia of trying to “cause a blackout”.

“America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements,” he said.

Speaking on NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday, Zelenskyy said that waiving sanctions against Russia would strengthen Putin’s war effort. He also said US-Ukraine intelligence sharing had resumed after being “blocked for some period of time”.

Zelenskyy said that while he trusted Trump, siding with Moscow would be a tragedy and a “historic mistake” for Washington.

Later on Sunday, Zelenskyy said on social media that he had spoken with US presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner about the results of an October 9 meeting between Washington and Kyiv’s negotiating teams in Miami, as well as the “next steps in diplomacy”.

Meanwhile, a Russian air strike ⁠killed ⁠a woman in the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, overnight while also hitting a subway station and damaging a 25-storey residential ⁠building, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram on Monday.

The attack, which also hit non-residential buildings and a medical facility, ‌injured three other people in Kyiv, Klitschko said.

Two Russian attacks on the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia killed a woman and wounded at least two other people, including a six-year-old girl, local officials said on Sunday.

In another post on X on Sunday, Zelenskyy said Russian strikes on residential buildings had killed two people and injured 12, including two children, in Volyn.

“This morning, there was a strike on an agricultural enterprise in Volyn. All necessary services are working at the site,” he said.

“In total, over this past week, the Russians have attacked Ukraine with almost 2,700 attack drones, 1,700 aerial bombs, and 66 missiles, most of them ballistic,” the Ukrainian president wrote.

articles.title: Strait of Hormuz crisis traps 6,000 sailors as attacks on ships mount, UN maritime chief says
articles.summary: Around 6,000 seafarers remain trapped near the Strait of Hormuz as 24 ships face attacks, while Iran accuses the U.S. military of using VHF Channel 16.
articles.body: Thousands of sailors remain stranded near the Strait of Hormuz amid escalating attacks on commercial ships, the United Nations' top maritime official warned Sunday after Iran accused the U.S. military of using an international emergency radio channel to threaten civilian crews. The warning also came amid reports that 24 ships had been attacked on the waterway over roughly two weeks, underscoring growing concerns about maritime safety in the region, according to Financial Times. "The situation continues to be severe and critical when it comes to international shipping," International Maritime Organization (IMO) Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez told Fox News Digital. "There is a double blockade and too many vessels have been attacked, particularly in recent days. 'VAST MAJORITY' OF IRAN'S ATTEMPTED ATTACKS ON STRAIT OF HORMUZ ARE UNSUCCESSFUL, CENTCOM SPOKESMAN SAYS "Seafarers have continued to perish in these attacks and around 6,000 seafarers remain trapped since the beginning of the conflict," he warned, adding that his message was not to transit the Strait of Hormuz or put seafarers at risk "until we have guarantees." Dominguez's warning followed an Oct. 9 letter to the IMO in which Iran alleged that the U.S. military used VHF Channel 16, an internationally designated maritime distress and safety channel, to intimidate Iranian crews in the Persian Gulf. "VHF Channel 16 has been repeatedly occupied for prolonged periods by the United States military forces operating in the Persian Gulf," the letter stated. TRUMP OPENS HORMUZ UNDER FIRE WITH ‘PROJECT FREEDOM’ AS IRAN WARNS OF ATTACKS "During such transmissions, Iranian seafarers have been addressed in Persian with threatening, abusive and provocative language and in certain instances urged to abandon their vessels." In a statement to Fox News Digital, U.S. Central Command defended its enforcement of the naval blockade of Iranian ports. "The U.S. naval blockade has been in place for months and is professionally communicated to all international mariners," CENTCOM said. "Vessels that refuse to comply with blockade enforcement receive multiple warnings, with ample opportunity to comply. "American forces remain highly vigilant, focused, and professional while fully enforcing the naval blockade against Iran." Iran's complaint was submitted by Seyed Ali Mousavi, its ambassador to the IMO, and circulated to member states on Oct. 9, according to a copy reviewed by Fox News Digital. Tehran also accused American forces of turning the maritime safety channel into an "instrument of military intimidation and psychological pressure against civilian crews." The letter cited commercial vessels, shipping companies and maritime operators but provided no recordings, transcripts or specific details of the alleged exchanges. Fox News Digital could not independently verify the accusations. IRAN THREATENS TO HALT RED SEA TRAFFIC IN RESPONSE TO US MILITARY BLOCKADE OF PORTS "Seafarers are not trained for combat, and they are not guilty of any conflicts that are happening around the world," Dominguez said. "And we have seen this in several parts of the world where Channel 16, that should not be used for this kind of communication, starts receiving messages that may be perceived as actually threatening or that are outside the remit of why it was created." Iran also asked the IMO to raise its allegations with member states and relevant international organizations, potentially including the International Telecommunication Union. Dominguez said the IMO could review its regulations and procedures to determine whether stronger safeguards are needed, though he did not announce a formal investigation. "Our role here at IMO is that when those situations take place, we will then look into any technical measures or any operational aspects that we may need to clarify further within our regulatory framework," he said, stressing that member states have equal rights to raise concerns, regardless of the conflict. "We have a responsibility, and I have a duty as well, to circulate letters and notes that the countries actually put forward when they're also being affected." WHO CONTROLS THE STRAIT OF HORMUZ RIGHT NOW? HERE'S WHAT THE SHIP TRAFFIC ACTUALLY SHOWS "We take all that information, meet at the level of different meetings of the organization and have the discussions," Dominguez added. "If it's demonstrated that we probably need to improve our rules in order to avoid communications issues, or that we need to enhance the knowledge of how these channels should be used, that is a role for us." The IMO had recorded 100 confirmed maritime incidents across the region as of Oct. 9, with 24 seafarers killed since the conflict began Feb. 28. Dominguez also warned that fraudulent ship registrations and false flags have become major contributors to the danger. articles.title: Arizona man accused of plotting mass casualty attack on religious site with 'cookbook' tied to OKC bombing
articles.summary: Prosecutors accused an Arizona man of keeping the Oklahoma City bombing-linked "Anarchist Cookbook" as his "Bible" while allegedly plotting a religious site attack.
articles.body: An Arizona man who allegedly plotted a mass casualty attack on a Jewish or Muslim house of worship is being accused by prosecutors of possessing an infamous bomb-making manual linked to the Oklahoma City bomber. Matthew Bjornholt, 27, faces a felony count of making a terrorist threat in connection with his alleged plot to attack a religious site. Prosecutors in Maricopa County said Bjornholt laid out a chilling blueprint for violence that involved guns, explosives and an accomplice tasked with gunning down survivors. During an initial court appearance on Friday, prosecutor Stephen Garcia sought a $500,000 cash bond, calling Bjornholt an imminent danger to the community, according to FOX 10. TRANS NEO-NAZI ACCUSED OF PLOTTING HINDU TEMPLE MASSACRE, WILL RECEIVE HORMONE TREATMENT IN JAIL: OFFICIALS Bjornholt allegedly outlined detailed plans to attack a religious site, according to Garcia, who also claimed the suspect kept a copy of "The Anarchist Cookbook," a manual containing bomb-making instructions that has been linked to Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh. Garcia alleged that Bjornholt referred to the book as his "Bible." The alleged plot included plans to detonate bombs before an accomplice of Bjornholt's would begin "picking off people" with firearms, according to prosecutors. Investigators later seized three guns and ammunition from Bjornholt’s home. Bjornholt’s defense attorney, Chad Schell, pushed back against the allegations, claiming that the charges are based solely on unverified hearsay from a disgruntled former acquaintance, according to FOX 10. Schell told the court that the tip came from a "homeless alcoholic" whom Bjornholt had briefly let crash on his couch before kicking him out late last month. PENNSYLVANIA MAN ACCUSED OF PLOTTING ISIS ATTACK ARRESTED WITH RIFLE AND 190 ROUNDS OF AMMUNITION: DOJ Schell said federal authorities had already investigated the claims weeks ago. Schell said the FBI executed a search warrant at Bjornholt’s home on Sept. 29 and that Bjornholt voluntarily provided investigators with his electronic devices and passwords. According to Schell, federal investigators found no evidence of terrorism or bomb-making materials and did not pursue federal charges before county authorities took over the case a couple of weeks later. "There is no evidence he's a danger to the community. What is the evidence that he's a danger to the community? Some hearsay statements from some dude — that my client kicked out of his house two days before September 29," Schell told the court. "Again, the FBI served a search warrant, got all of his electronic devices. He gave them access, gave him his passwords to those devices. They went through all of those electronic devices. They didn't see anything about terrorism. And FBI cut him loose," he continued. Schell also argued that the three seized guns were lawfully possessed, adding that Bjornholt's civil rights were restored after completing a previous sentence on a drug charge stemming from a closed first-degree murder case. According to Schell, the murder charge against Bjornholt was dropped because of a lack of evidence. The ammunition found inside the home, Schell said, was no more than standard magazine loads. Despite prosecutors citing Bjornholt's criminal history in arguing for a larger bond, the judge said the state's preliminary evidence relied heavily on hearsay and set Bjornholt's bond at $100,000, according to FOX 10. The judge nevertheless found enough probable cause to move the case forward. It remains unclear whether specific houses of worship were targeted in the alleged plot or whether there was a specific accomplice. Bjornholt is scheduled to return to court on Oct. 22 for a status conference and then later for a preliminary hearing on Oct. 26.

articles.title: ‘No conclusive evidence’ of Amelia Earhart’s missing plane found in South Pacific expedition
articles.summary: The expedition said the anomaly captured on satellite imagery, hypothesized to be wreckage of Earhart’s plane, was most likely “a collection of debris.”
articles.body: An expedition to find evidence of Amelia Earhart’s missing plane near a remote island in the South Pacific has come up empty, researchers said Sunday. Researchers from the Archaeological Legacy Institute and Purdue University embarked this month on the Taraia Object expedition in Nikumaroro, an uninhabited coral atoll in the Phoenix Islands belonging to the Republic of Kiribati. The team sought to identify an anomaly first seen in satellite images in 2020. Experts have long suspected Nikumaroro as the landing site of Earhart and her navigator, Fred Noonan, who disappeared in July 1937. However, the expedition “found no conclusive evidence to confirm a hypothesis that wreckage” from Earhart’s plane was “in a lagoon on a remote atoll in the South Pacific,” the university said in a news release. “We think it’s most likely that the object was a collection of debris that accumulated here,” Rick Pettigrew, ALI’s executive director, said in a video message. The expedition determined that the anomaly was most “likely a collection of large trees deposited along the peninsula’s sandpit.” When the team arrived, much of the “debris had fragmented and washed away.” What was left was a Y-shaped segment that was just a small fraction of the anomaly’s original size observed via satellite. The anomaly’s reflective surface, which was “long associated with the idea that the object was a metallic substance,” was found to be a carbonate veneer, meaning it had a layer of carbon-rich sediment. “We accomplished our goal to determine what the Taraia Object was,” Pettigrew said. “Our team remains in great spirits and proud of what was accomplished.” Earhart was seeking to be the first woman to fly around the world when she and Noonan disappeared in their Lockheed Electra 10-E. A U.S. Coast Guard ship lost contact with the pair the morning of July 2, 1937, as they tried to fly to Howland Island, about 400 miles northwest of Nikumaroro. The expedition to find Earhart’s plane launched from Tarawa in the Republic of Kiribati on Oct. 6 and traveled for five days by sea to Nikumaroro. While it didn’t crack one of the world’s greatest mysteries, the expedition said the effort strongly supports the broader castaway hypothesis — a theory that Earhart and Noonan didn’t crash into the sea but landed on the flat reef of Nikumaroro and were marooned. Some artifacts found on the island indicate Earhart and Noonan’s plane may have landed there, including glass bottles from the 1930s and a woman’s makeup compact, the expedition said. It said it did find “numerous artifacts through both maritime and terrestrial archaeology efforts, including a steel tube about 30 inches long discovered in the lagoon near the Taraia Peninsula,” which will be further studied. “Amelia Earhart never gave up — she kept pushing boundaries and flying into the unknown,” Steve Schultz, Purdue’s general counsel and an expedition member, said in a statement. “That same fire fuels our search. She kept flying, and we will keep searching.”

articles.title: Shakahola cult leader Paul Mackenzie faces Kenya charges over 52 further deaths
articles.summary: Prosecutors say Paul Mackenzie lured the latest victims to their deaths by writing notes from his prison cell.
articles.body:
A Kenyan court is set to deliver a judgement in a mass murder case involving doomsday preacher Paul Mackenzie.

Mackenzie and 29 of his followers are being charged with the murder of 191 children.

His cult is alleged to have forced children to starve to death so that they could "meet Jesus". His doomsday doctrine said that education was forbidden and modern medicine was considered "evil".

Mackenzie and the 29 others have all pleaded not guilty to murder, repeatedly insisting that nobody was forced to die.

Mackenzie's former head of security, Enos Amanya Ngala, was initially accused but then entered a plea deal and became a witness for the prosecution.

Mackenzie and other leaders of the cult are facing a raft of other legal cases, including for terrorism, radicalisation and denying education to children.

But this is the first time the pastor will face a verdict on the most serious charges of murder.

Authorities said over 400 bodies were found in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast, where Mackenzie led his followers from across the country.

Seventeen men were hired from the nearby town for the horrifying task of digging up the shallow graves. Some were paid just $8 (£6) a day.

"Every grave we found had at least three bodies," James, one of the gravediggers, told the BBC. "Some of the remains were of children as young as a few weeks old."

"We once found 12 bodies of children in a line inside a grave. It was massive, the bodies were arranged like clothes. One on top of another."

Gravediggers described some of the bodies of children as having had their "hands and legs tied and bodies wrapped in bedsheets".

Although many of Mackenzie's followers were from elsewhere in Kenya, some of the remains are of people who were familiar to the community because the people in the cult would often go to nearby Shakahola town for supplies and to fetch water from the River Galana which flows through the town.

"We would sometimes carry people on our motorbikes into the forest," said Salim Karisa, another gravedigger. "But it was so planned and secretive that nobody could tell what was happening inside."

Stephen Mwiti, 48, recounted losing all six of his children to the cult and seeing "many bald women and tens of children" surrounding Mackenzie in his house when he went to confront him. Mackenzie forbade make-up and hairstyles, so told women to shave off their hair or keep it unkempt.

Mwiti's former wife is one of those accused alongside Mackenzie.

"If I met Pastor Mackenzie today, one of us will have to die," told the BBC.

"All six of my children died in Shakahola forest," Mwiti said, visibly emotional holding a photograph of his family. "I only found and buried the remains of my son Samuel."

"This little thing here was the start of all my misery," Mwiti said as he pointed at a dusty TV and cable box in his home in the coastal town of Malindi, 70km (43 miles) from Shakahola. It was from that TV that Mackenzie's doctrine made it to his home.

The pastor established Good News International Ministries in 2003. Over the next 16 years, the church grew in popularity to draw thousands of followers in the church's branches across Kenya.

His church ran a television station called Times TV which would broadcast his sermons from his church in Malindi.

His End Days sermons included conspiracy theories that described education as "evil", healthcare as "against the doctrine" and digital identity cards as "the mark of the devil".

Mackenzie's son, Dan Paul Mackenzie, said he worked as a cameraperson in the church. "The children would sit at the back, adults in the middle, and everyone would sing worship songs all morning."

The pastor would start his fiery sermons at noon, some of which included "casting out demons".

The main church shut down in 2019 and Paul Mackenzie moved to Shakahola forest, encouraging his devotees to follow him.

Peter Shukrani, 23, says his mother relocated to Shakahola with him at the time. He started going to Mackenzie's church when he was eight years old and described him as his "spiritual father", adding that he would "never say a bad word about him".

When in the forest, Shukrani fell ill and his condition deteriorated because medication was banned.

"My mother would throw away all the medicine I was supposed to take because she believe that only God could heal me," Shukrani said.

The community was described as mud houses scattered across the vast forest. "We lived a quiet normal life, fasting for a few days then having a small meal," Shukrani said.

By March 2023 when the first remains were discovered by local herders, hundreds of people had died. "We would carry someone out of the forest but they were so frail that they would die in our arms," explained Salim Karisa, one of the gravediggers.

Shukrani was one of the men rescued from the forest in March 2023.

He was ill and bed-ridden for weeks until that point, but his condition worsened because his mother would throw away all the medication he needed to recover.

"My mother believed Pastor Mackenzie's doctrine that medicine was evil," Shukrani said.

"I would have died if I wasn't rescued from Shakahola forest."

In the 298 pages detailing the charges against him in the current case, all of the 191 victims Mackenzie and his followers are accused of murdering are children.

Many of the bodies are still unidentified, owing to their advanced state of decomposition.

In the court documents, several are referred to as "unknown male child" and identified by the location of their grave and date of their discovery.

Despite the suffering endured by Mackenzie's followers, men, women and children who died due to starvation, strangulation and even being bludgeoned to death, as well as his own suffering, Shukrani believes Mackenzie was "a good person who cares for me".

"Mackenzie didn't force anyone to fast. People made those choices by themselves because of their beliefs," Shukrani said.

"I still love him and he is still my pastor."

In contrast Dan Mackenzie believes his father should be found guilty of murder.

"He was the leader, he was someone who they were looking [up to]. So he is a murderer of mass killing."

Ravana's effigies are burnt and people exchange greetings.What if the Ravana we need to defeat is within us.It could be our anger, the habit of postponing decisions, an unhealthy attachment or even the constant need for approval.This Vijayadashami comes with an interesting planetary backdrop. With your ruling planet Mars debilitated in Cancer, emotional reactions deserve attention. This Vijayadashami, make a conscious effort to respond rather than react. Walk away from one unnecessary argument. Sometimes, maintaining peace is a bigger victory.Taurus: Win Over Your AttachmentThere may be a relationship, possession or familiar routine that you continue holding on to simply because it has been part of your life for years. With Venus retrograde, reconsider what still brings genuine happiness. This doesn't mean abandoning people or responsibilities. It means recognising the difference between love and attachment.Gemini: Win Over Your IndecisionYou may have several ideas, multiple options and plenty of advice from others. Yet the decision remains pending. This Vijayadashami, choose one matter you have been postponing and take a practical step towards resolving it. You don't need complete certainty before every decision. Sometimes, clarity comes only after you begin.Cancer: Win Over Emotional ExhaustionYou may have become everyone's problem-solver without realising how much it is costing you. Jupiter in Cancer encourages generosity, but debilitated Mars can make emotional pressure harder to manage. This Vijayadashami, stop taking responsibility for situations you cannot control.Leo: Win Over Your EgoThere is a difference between self-respect and expecting everyone to acknowledge your importance. With the Sun debilitated in Libra, you may need to reconsider how you respond when your opinions are challenged. Listen to someone you would normally dismiss. Accepting a better suggestion doesn't diminish your authority. It shows confidence.Virgo: Win Over PerfectionismHow many things have you postponed because the timing, preparation or circumstances were not perfect? Your attention to detail is valuable, but it can occasionally prevent progress. This Vijayadashami, complete something that has been waiting for your final approval. Not every task needs another round of corrections.Libra: Win Over People-PleasingYou may have spent considerable time keeping everyone comfortable while ignoring what you actually want. With the Sun and retrograde Venus in Libra, personal expectations and relationships deserve a fresh look. This Vijayadashami, say no to one commitment you genuinely cannot accommodate. Being considerate does not mean agreeing with everyone.Scorpio: Win Over ResentmentAn old disagreement may still influence how you see someone, even if the incident happened months or years ago. This Vijayadashami, ask yourself whether holding on to that anger is helping you. Forgiveness doesn't require rebuilding the relationship or pretending nothing happened. Sometimes, it simply means refusing to let an old experience control your present.Sagittarius: Win Over the Need to Be RightYour knowledge and experience may help others, but not everyone will follow your advice. With Jupiter exalted in Cancer, this is an opportunity to practise wisdom alongside patience. This Vijayadashami, allow someone to make a different choice without turning it into a debate. This Vijayadashami, give yourself permission to pause without feeling guilty. Rest is not the opposite of ambition.Aquarius: Win Over Emotional DistanceYou may be comfortable discussing ideas, plans and possibilities, but less comfortable expressing what you actually feel. This can leave people close to you guessing. This Vijayadashami, initiate one honest conversation you have been avoiding. You don't have to reveal everything, but a little emotional openness can strengthen an important relationship.Pisces: Win Over Self-DoubtYou will question your abilities or waiting for someone to reassure you before taking the next step. With Saturn moving through Pisces, responsibilities can sometimes feel heavier than expected. This Vijayadashami, acknowledge how much you have already managed. articles.title: China’s economy accelerates on robust exports as domestic weakness persists
articles.summary: China said Monday that its economy grew 4.5% for the July-September quarter from a year ago fueled by robust exports, moving closer to meeting its official annual growth target as the year nears its end.
articles.body: HONG KONG — China said Monday that its economy grew 4.5% for the July-September quarter from a year earlier fueled by robust exports, moving closer to meeting its official annual growth target as the year nears its end and at a time when its trading partners feel an increased urgency in balancing their trade deficits with the world’s second-biggest economy. The better-than-expected official data accelerated from the 4.3% year-on-year growth recorded in the April-June quarter, which was the slowest expansion in more than three years. For the whole year, Chinese leaders have set a growth target of 4.5% to 5%, down from last year’s 5% expansion. Earlier this month, the International Monetary Fund trimmed its forecast for China’s 2026 economic growth to 4.5%, just meeting the lower end of Beijing’s goal. The headline official growth figure is becoming “an increasingly poor indicator of how the broader economy is performing,” said Max Zenglein, Asia-Pacific senior economist at the Conference Board. That’s because it masks “widening disparities across industries, regions and households,” Zenglein said. Beijing faces difficult trade-offs, and managing domestic imbalances may prove more challenging than dealing with external pressures, he said. China’s domestic demand has weakened, weighed down by a yearslong downturn in its property market that has squeezed household wealth and driven up savings. Still, with strong exports being one of the few bright spots, China is on track to surpass last year’s record $1.2 trillion trade surplus globally, after logging 36% growth in exports last month and already a $938 billion surplus from January to September. Elevated U.S. tariffs have hit some U.S.-China bilateral trade and forced China to look elsewhere, including Southeast Asia, Latin America and Europe. High-tech exports such as semiconductors and autos, including hybrid and electric vehicles, are among areas driving its export growth this year. As China pursues self-sufficiency to help shield itself from Western export controls and trade uncertainties, it has built up massive domestic manufacturing capacities across industries such as solar and EVs that were also heavily subsidized by the government. But output was scaled up rapidly at a time of weakened domestic consumption, so many of these goods are shipped to overseas markets at competitive pricing. An export-reliant growth model that is highly tech-driven has shown limited job creation and broad income gains while risks of artificial intelligence-driven labor displacements continue to grow, said Ecaterina Bigos, senior market strategist at BNP Paribas Asset Management. Many of China’s trade partners fear their domestic industries and economies face growing threats from the surge of lower-cost Chinese manufactured imports. “It is untenable and unsustainable for the world’s second-largest economy to rely on foreign demand to prop up its own growth,” said Eswar Prasad, a professor of economics and trade policy at Cornell University. Through its persistent and large trade surpluses, China “has become a drag on world growth rather than an engine that pulls the rest of the world along,” Prasad said. The European Union is among those impatient to reduce its trade imbalance with China. The 27-nation bloc runs a trade deficit with China of more than $1.1 billion a day. For the first nine months of the year, Chinese exports to the E.U. were up 16%. E.U. countries are eyeing more curbs on China after the bloc reached an agreement with China this month to roughly halve the number of Chinese hybrid vehicle imports over the next few years. China can work with other countries on disputes, and it wants to keep its market access, said Gary Ng, a senior economist for Asia-Pacific at French bank Natixis. With a deal with the E.U. on hybrid cars, for example, China can most likely still sell more made-by-China products to its economies in the longer run while avoiding a broad tariff increase. But even with agreements made between China and the E.U., “trade imbalances will be difficult to resolve quickly,” said Lynn Song, chief economist for Greater China at Dutch bank ING. Policymakers also argue that an undervalued yuan, China’s currency, against the dollar and the euro has contributed to China’s growing trade surplus, even though China’s central bank has dismissed the claims. “We are likely to see continued resistance, rising protectionism, and persistent pressure from economies globally to protect their industries, and jobs, notably in high-value sectors,” Bigos said. Beijing has insisted that China does not seek a large trade surplus. On Friday, China’s central bank governor Pan Gongsheng said countries with trade deficits and those with trade surpluses should work together, and that China, as a responsible country, has been committed to expanding domestic demand.

articles.title: France's government under pressure after weekend of widespread violence
articles.summary: Political tension grips France after rioting marred protests over the cost of living and struggling public services, Katya Adler writes.
articles.body:
France's Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu is holding a crisis cabinet meeting on Monday to assess a weekend of violence and looting across the country, in what were some of the worst scenes of public disorder in modern French history.

On Saturday over half a million mainly peaceful protesters demonstrated against rising living costs and dwindling access to decent public services, including a good state education. But the protests turned nasty after groups of black-clad, masked activists and vandals appeared.

An estimated 1,500 shops and businesses were looted and destroyed. Riot police fired tear gas and turned water cannon on crowds. They were seen hitting people with batons in several places. France's interior ministry said about 1,000 police officers were injured on Saturday, seven of them seriously.

There had been rumours in France that President Emmanuel Macron may introduce a temporary curfew in parts of the country, or even impose a state of emergency to help calm the febrile atmosphere. In the end, he used a televised address to the nation on Sunday to call for national unity and to try to assure the French public that the perpetrators of the violence would be punished.

Macron's speech has been roundly criticised on social media forums and by political opponents for lacking concrete detail.

How will vandals and rioters now be brought to account?

How might France's towns and cities be better protected - especially since new mass demonstrations have been announced in a couple of weeks' time?

Exactly how will destroyed businesses be compensated?

And when will a dialogue be established with students and teachers' bodies on the subject of education?

On Sunday the Secretary General of the CGT union, Sophie Binet, accused Macron of failing to address students' concerns, the cost-of-living crisis or the dwindling quality of public services in France.

He's apparently passed that baton to Prime Minister Lecornu. Yet he and his interior minister are charged by many in France with being woefully ill-prepared and under-policed ahead of Saturday's multiple, scheduled protests.

The president of France's lower house of parliament, Yaël Braun-Pivet, says she wants to open an inquiry into exactly what happened this weekend and why.

"Things are dark in the city of light [a nickname for Paris]" was the graffiti I read daubed in red paint across a wall adjacent to a row of shattered shops in the French capital on Sunday night.

Macron is widely viewed here as a lame-duck president. He is on his way out. There's a hotly contested race under way to become his successor, with the vote scheduled in six months' time. The presidential candidate from the anti-immigration nationalist right (Marine Le Pen) and also the anti-capitalist left (Jean-Luc Melenchon) are vying to make headlines.

That is adding to current tensions in France - in politics as well as on the streets.

Parliament here is paralysed, deeply divided between three vying political blocks.

Then there are France's financial woes too. Investors are leaning hard on this country to get its spiralling public debt under control. But the French government worries, if it cuts public services or welfare, yet more angry people will pour out onto the streets.

What now, what next, is our country broken? You hear these questions a lot at the moment.

People across France were shocked and troubled by Saturday's events. The images of tear-gassed towns, apparently unimpeded looters and burning public buildings have worried the nation.

Many passers-by I speak to express frustration that, while they worry about the future, their leading politicians seem, instead, to be passionately focused on finger-pointing; blaming one another for the volatility.

"While we worry for our safety, they use this situation as a pre-presidential election political football," teacher and father of three Edouard told me.

Macron and his prime minister blamed Saturday's violent chaos on radical far left groups and delinquents; hard left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon alleged government "incompetence"; Marine Le Pen on the nationalist right, which likes to be seen as strong on law and order, posted a video seated in front of the French flag, giving a presidential-style address blaming the "Macronist administration that is out of steam, exhausted, and disoriented".

For the next two weeks, the French authorities hope for a bit of a respite. Students start their half-term break as of Monday.

But on 5 November, a cross-section of trade unions, plus France's disparate "yellow jacket" (gilets jaunes) movement that staged demonstrations for over a year in 2018 - during Macron's first term as president - have announced huge protests.

articles.title: Witnesses haunted by what they saw when pickup plowed through a Kansas youth soccer game
articles.summary: The crash at Stryker Sports Complex in Wichita killed a 6-year-old boy and a 35-year-old man and injured several children and adults.
articles.body: Witnesses of Saturday’s deadly collision in which a pickup truck barreled through a youth soccer game in Kansas, killing two people and injuring nearly a dozen others, said they are haunted by what they saw and heard. Cole Adrian, 6, and Nicholas Schafer, 35, were killed in the incident, which unfolded shortly before 3:30 p.m. at the city-owned Stryker Sports Complex in Wichita, police said. The deceased were both from McPherson, Kansas, but were not related to each other, a Wichita police spokesperson said. Ten other people, ages 5 to 68, were also hit and hospitalized with non-life-threatening injuries, Police Capt. Aaron Moses said. Police said a dark Chevrolet pickup drove onto a field during a youth soccer game and struck children and adults. Erica Case said it was halftime during her 9-year-old son’s soccer game on an adjacent field when she first heard an engine revving, followed by several “boom” sounds. “I saw the truck hitting things. I saw debris flying in the air,” she recalled. “I don’t know if it was a cone, a chair or a person, but you could see matter flying as the truck was barreling through the soccer field at a decent rate of speed.” She said the sound will haunt her. “The moment that I recognized that that wasn’t gunshots, that that was bodies, I lost it,” Case said. “I lost it because it wasn’t just adults. It was also children.” Case recalled the mother of another boy shouting that she was a nurse and needed to get to the injured. Case said she told her she would watch her boy and then took the woman’s son to safety amid the chaos. It took about 10 minutes for emergency services to arrive, she said, but people began helping the victims during that time. “There are a lot of silent heroes that I know experienced much worse than I did, having to do mouth-to-mouth or CPR on somebody that’d been ran over by a truck,” Case said. David Griekspoor was at the complex with his nephew, who also plays soccer, when he witnessed the incident. “It sounded like small gunfire,” he said. “Bap, bap, bap.” He said it wasn’t clear what was producing the sound until he focused on the truck. “You look up, and you just see the truck going through a line of people,” Griekspoor said. He said his brother and sister-in-law went to check on children nearby as he grabbed his nephew and “backed out of there.” All ended up safe, Griekspoor said. Police said they interviewed more than 30 witnesses. The pickup’s driver, a 34-year-old woman from Garden City, Kansas, was taken into custody but was later released after police consulted with the Sedgwick County District Attorney’s Office. She has not been charged with a crime and has not been identified. Police said the woman, who had two children in the pickup, had a child who had a soccer game on a different field at the complex. The driver was cooperating with officers, said Moses, the police captain. What caused the pickup to drive through the field was still under investigation, and police said the results of an examination of the vehicle, as well as of toxicology testing on the driver, were pending.

articles.title: Air India offloaded a passenger over his covid test report in 2021; Amritsar consumer commission orders airline to pay Rs 50,000 for mental agony, harassment
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Amritsar district consumer commission has directed Air India to pay Rs 50,000 to a passenger who could not board his London flight in March
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Amritsar district consumer commission has directed Air India to pay Rs 50,000 to a passenger who could not board his London flight in March 2021, citing deficiency in service. The commission awarded Rs 40,000 as compensation and Rs 10,000 towards litigation costs.The commission found that the airlines’ officials had failed to properly guide the passenger regarding covid-19 travel requirements. However, it rejected passenger's claims for a refund of the original airfare and reimbursement of testing, quarantine and subsequent ticket expenses.Air India boarding disputeAccording to the commission order, Surinder Singh, the complainant, booked a flight on March 14, 2021, to travel from Amritsar to Heathrow, London, via Mumbai. He paid Rs 28,919 for the journey scheduled for March 19, 2021.Singh alleged that he obtained a negative RT-PCR report from an ICMR-accredited laboratory and deposited 210 pounds, equivalent to Rs 21,773, towards Covid-19 testing and quarantine requirements in the UK.The complainant claimed that he reached Amritsar airport well before departure and showed the airline officials his passport, visa, negative RT-PCR report and a message from the Punjab government regarding his test. However, the ground staff and station manager allegedly refused to let him board without satisfactorily explaining the reason.After the flight departed, the officials returned his ticket with an endorsement referring to the absence of a message confirming the RT-PCR sample collection. Singh subsequently bought another ticket for Rs 19,000.He approached the consumer commission seeking a refund of Rs 28,919 towards airfare, Rs 21,773 towards Covid-19 testing and quarantine expenses, Rs 2 lakh as compensation and Rs 22,000 as litigation costs.The airline denied deficiency in service, arguing that Singh’s RT-PCR report did not specify the sample collection time, making it difficult to establish compliance with the 72-hour requirement. They also claimed he had not submitted the UK passenger locator form.It alleged that the complainant was advised to travel from Amritsar to Mumbai and complete the remaining formalities there but refused and was marked as having voluntarily opted for self-offloading. They also argued that the travel agency through which he booked the tickets should have been made a party to the complaint.Commission's finding on Air IndiaThe bench comprising President Jagdishwar Kumar Chopra and member Mandeep Kaur found that the airlines had failed to establish that Singh received a clear explanation of the deficiencies in his documents or adequate assistance to complete the formalities.“The plea taken by the opposite parties that the complainant was ‘self-offloaded’ does not, by itself, completely absolve the opposite parties of their obligation to provide reasonable assistance to their passenger,” the commission said.It also noted that the airlines had not produced sufficient evidence to show that Singh was given a clear written explanation of the documentation requirements he had allegedly failed to meet.“The allegations of the complainant regarding the conduct of the officials, though not sufficient to establish all the reliefs claimed, do indicate that he was not dealt with in a manner expected from a professional airline service provider,” the bench said.The commission held that the airlines’ failure to guide and assist Singh regarding the applicable travel requirements amounted to deficiency in service.However, it rejected his claim for a refund of Rs 28,919, finding that the evidence did not establish that the airlines had completely and unjustifiably denied him the opportunity to travel.The commission also refused to reimburse Rs 21,773 towards Covid-19 testing and quarantine expenses, observing that Singh had not established a sufficient direct link between this expenditure and the deficiency proved against the airlines. It rejected the claim for Rs 19,000 spent on the subsequent ticket, noting that he had undertaken the journey for which it was purchased.Considering the inconvenience, mental agony and harassment Singh suffered, the commission awarded Rs 40,000 as compensation and Rs 10,000 towards litigation costs. It dismissed the complaint against the Airport Authority of India.What did the commission order?The commission, in its October 6, 2026 order, partly allowed the complaint and directed Air India and Air India Ltd to:Pay Rs 40,000 as compensation for mental agony, harassment and inconvenience.Pay Rs 10,000 towards litigation costs.Comply with the order within 45 days of receiving a copy.The commission did not order a refund of the original airfare or reimbursement of the other travel-related expenses.

articles.title: Lula and Bolsonaro spar in Brazil’s fiery first presidential run-off debate
articles.summary: Brazil’s president and his opponent lob a barrage of attacks on each other in debate a week before the October 25 vote.
articles.body:
Brazil’s President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro fired off a barrage of personal attacks during their first debate a week before a tight presidential run-off.

In a chaotic exchange on Sunday, the two men called each other “liar” multiple times, accused each other of corruption, dragged up various scandals, and clashed on issues from public security to healthcare.

Lula said Bolsonaro was “a habitual liar” and a “thug”, and physically distanced himself on stage from the candidate he called a “militiaman”, alluding to his alleged ties to Rio de Janeiro’s paramilitary groups.

Bolsonaro, who led the first-round election with 47 percent to Lula’s 45 percent, said it was better to keep Lula at a distance “because my wallet could be stolen”.

Throughout the debate, Bolsonaro, 45, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, paced behind Lula, shaking his head, smirking and scoffing as his adversary spoke.

The 80-year-old Lula, who is seeking a fourth term, demanded an explanation regarding a corruption investigation involving the older Bolsonaro, a question his opponent dodged.

The younger Bolsonaro responded by calling Lula a “clown”, and then parried by bringing up a potential corruption case involving one of the president’s sons.

Jair Bolsonaro has been under house arrest while serving a 27-year sentence connected to efforts to overturn the 2022 election, which he lost to Lula.

Cost of living, public spending in focus

Flavio Bolsonaro hammered away at the top concerns of Brazilians, such as the cost of living and crime, and accused Lula of “reckless spending” to get re-elected, referring to various social measures the president has announced during the campaign.

Lula countered by asking Bolsonaro about his plans to emulate the drastic public spending cuts implemented by Argentina’s right-wing president, Javier Milei.

Bolsonaro dodged the question throughout the debate and pivoted to different topics.

When his father’s handling of the COVID-19 pandemic came up, Bolsonaro admitted that this “wasn’t an area where we saw the best results during Bolsonaro’s presidency. I’ll offer a mea culpa here.”

Lula also sought to portray his opponent as out of touch with poor Brazilians, saying Bolsonaro had never used the country’s public healthcare system or taken a bus.

“My opponent only knows about buses from books. He has never even stepped foot on one. He has no idea what the world of work is like,” Lula said.

Ahead of Sunday’s debate, supporters of each candidate gathered en masse in public to show their allegiance.

Pro-Bolsonaro crowds wearing Brazil’s national colours of yellow, green and blue packed Paulista Avenue in Sao Paulo’s financial centre, where the candidate addressed the crowd.
